content: The document outlines detailed medical guidelines and algorithms for cervical cancer screening, triage, and treatment, with specific recommendations for different populations, including women living with HIV. 1. Screen-and-Treat Approach: In this approach, treatment decisions are based solely on a positive result from the primary screening test. No additional confirmatory tests are required before initiating treatment. 2. Screen, Triage, and Treat Approach: This method involves a primary screening test followed by a secondary triage test. Treatment is initiated only if both tests yield positive results. Histological confirmation may or may not be required depending on the setting. 3. Primary VIA Screening (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid): Women undergo VIA as the primary screening test. If the result is positive, eligibility for ablative treatment is assessed. Ablative treatments include cryotherapy or thermal ablation. If ineligible for ablation, LLETZ (Large-Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone) or CKC (Cold Knife Conization) is performed. Women with suspected cancer are referred for further evaluation, biopsy, and management. Follow-up occurs one year post-treatment, and rescreening is recommended every three years. 4. Primary HPV DNA Testing (Screen-and-Treat Approach): HPV DNA testing, either self-collected or clinician-collected, is used as the primary screening test. Positive results lead to assessment for ablative treatment eligibility. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted after one year, and rescreening is recommended every 5–10 years for the general population and every 3–5 years for women living with HIV. 5. Primary Cytology Screening with Colposcopy Triage: Cytology (conventional or liquid-based) is used as the primary screening test. Women with abnormal cytology results (e.g., ASCUS or worse) undergo immediate triage with HPV testing. HPV-positive cases are referred for colposcopy, and further management is based on colposcopy or histopathology findings. Rescreening is recommended every three years. 6. HPV DNA Screening with HPV 16/18 Triage: HPV DNA testing is the primary screening test. Women testing positive for HPV 16/18 are assessed for ablative treatment eligibility. Those testing positive for other high-risk HPV types undergo VIA triage. Post-treatment follow-up occurs after one year, and rescreening intervals are the same as in the primary HPV DNA testing approach. 7. HPV DNA Screening with VIA Triage: HPV DNA testing is the primary screening test. Women testing positive undergo VIA triage. If VIA is negative, repeat HPV testing is performed after two years for the general population or one year for women living with HIV. Positive VIA results lead to treatment eligibility assessment. Follow-up occurs one year post-treatment. 8. HPV DNA Screening with Cytology Triage Followed by Colposcopy: HPV DNA testing is the primary screening test. Women testing positive undergo cytology triage. If cytology results are abnormal (e.g., ASCUS or worse), colposcopy is performed. Management is based on colposcopy or histopathology findings. Rescreening intervals are the same as in other HPV DNA-based approaches. 9. Post-Treatment Follow-Up: Women treated with ablation or LLETZ without histopathology results, or those treated based on histopathology findings of CIN 2/3 or AIS, undergo follow-up testing within 12 months. Negative follow-up results allow return to routine screening intervals. Positive results necessitate further evaluation, biopsy, and possible retreatment. 10. Transformation Zone Assessment: The transformation zone (TZ) is classified into three types based on visibility and location: Type 1: Entire TZ is visible and ectocervical. Type 2: Entire TZ is visible but includes an endocervical component. Type 3: TZ is not fully visible and extends into the endocervical canal. Eligibility for treatment is determined by visualizing the cervix after applying 3–5% acetic acid, with or without magnification. Histological diagnosis is not mandatory. 11. Special Considerations for Women Living with HIV: Screening and follow-up intervals are shorter for women living with HIV due to their higher risk of cervical cancer progression. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted within 12 months, and rescreening is recommended every 3–5 years. 12. Treatment Modalities: Ablative treatments include cryotherapy and thermal ablation. LLETZ and LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) are used interchangeably. CKC is an alternative if LLETZ is unavailable. In settings without histology, women are advised to attend follow-up after one year or earlier if symptoms of cervical cancer develop. 13. Resource and Infrastructure Constraints: The availability of interventions such as LLETZ or safe surgical settings may limit treatment options. Feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and resources are critical factors influencing the implementation of these guidelines. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the cervical cancer screening and treatment guidelines, ensuring clarity for medical professionals.
